theme: Ezra arrives; the journey from Babylon to Jerusalem
readingInstruction: Read Ezra 7:1-8:36. Fifty-eight years after the temple is finished, Ezra the scribe arrives in Jerusalem. Notice what the text says about his heart in 7:10, and how he organizes the journey in chapter 8.
settingTheScene: Ezra comes to Jerusalem in 458 BC, in the seventh year of Artaxerxes. He is a priest descended from Aaron and a scribe skilled in the Law of Moses. The temple was built, but the community was spiritually weak, and many were not following the law. The king gave Ezra authority to teach and enforce it. He leads a second group of returning exiles, about 1,800 people.
observation: “This Ezra went up from Babylonia. He was a scribe skilled in the Law of Moses” (7:6).
“And the king granted him all that he asked, for the hand of the LORD his God was on him” (7:6).
“For Ezra had set his heart to study the Law of the LORD, and to do it and to teach his statutes and rules in Israel” (7:10).
“Blessed be the LORD, the God of our fathers, who put such a thing as this into the heart of the king” (7:27).
“I was ashamed to ask the king for a band of soldiers and horsemen to protect us against the enemy on the way” (8:22).
“The hand of our God is for good on all who seek him, and the power of his wrath is against all who forsake him” (8:22).
“So we fasted and implored our God for this, and he listened to our entreaty” (8:23).
“The hand of our God was on us, and he delivered us from the hand of the enemy and from ambushes by the way” (8:31).
interpretation:
Verse 10 of chapter 7 is among the best descriptions of a teacher of God’s word in the Bible. Ezra “set his heart” to do three things in order: to study the Law of the LORD, to do it, and to teach it. First he studied. Second he practiced. Only then did he teach. The order matters. A teacher who has not studied is shallow. A teacher who has not obeyed is a hypocrite. And study and obedience exist for the sake of sharing.

The phrase “the hand of the LORD his God was on him” appears again and again. Ezra does not take credit. The king’s favor, the safe journey, the gifts and authority all come from God’s hand. The letter from Artaxerxes is remarkable: it commands the treasurers to give whatever Ezra requests for the house of the God of heaven, “lest his wrath be against the realm of the king.” Again, the heart of a Persian king is in God’s hand.

Chapter 8 gives the list of the families and the preparation for the journey. Ezra gathers the people at the river Ahava and discovers that no Levites have come. He sends for them, and they come. Then he does something striking. He is ashamed to ask the king for an armed escort, since he had told the king that “the hand of our God is for good on all who seek him.” Having said it, he proves it. The group fasts and prays for a safe journey. “And he listened to our entreaty.” The caravan carries a fortune in silver, gold, and vessels, and they are not robbed.

The principle is that faith is shown in dependence. Ezra could have asked for soldiers. He chose prayer. He took a risk, the kind that invites God to show who he is.
connection: 2 Timothy 2:15 says, “Do your best to present yourself to God as one approved, a worker who has no need to be ashamed, rightly handling the word of truth.” James 1:22 says to be doers of the word. Ezekiel 3:1-3 shows the prophet eating the scroll. Ezra’s study, practice, and teaching match Jesus’ pattern (Acts 1:1). Psalm 20:7: “Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God.”
application:
Follow Ezra’s order: study something in Scripture this week, apply it, and then share it with someone.

Think about when you reached for “soldiers and horsemen” instead of prayer. What would it look like to depend on God in that area?

Give thanks for those who teach God’s word faithfully.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to give you a heart set to study his law, do it, and teach it.
Ask him to let his hand be on you for good.
Tell him where you are trusting him over human protection.
